segments.title: Why 11-inch guns did not make Scharnhorst a battlecruiser
segments.body: Scharnhorst and Gneisenau show why main-gun calibre alone cannot classify a warship. Germany wanted 15-inch weapons, but contemporary industry could supply only 11-inch guns, so the installed battery was a constraint rather than the design's defining purpose. Their armour, internal subdivision, speed, and overall arrangement support treating them as fast battleships. This watch point weighs the whole design and intended role instead of treating one specification as decisive.

evidence.note: The introduction explains that Scharnhorst and Gneisenau were fast battleships whose 11-inch guns reflected German industrial limits rather than a battlecruiser role.

segments.summary: Scharnhorst and Gneisenau show why gun calibre alone cannot classify a capital ship: protection, subdivision, speed, and intended role also matter.

segments.title: Why bigger naval guns were not automatically better
segments.body: The 16.5-inch or 420 mm gun recurs in unbuilt capital-ship designs because it promised more effect than a 16-inch weapon without the steeper handling penalty of still larger shells. An impressive initial firing cycle differs from the sustained rate a turret and crew could maintain after ready ammunition was expended. That distinction matters because heavier projectiles and machinery slow the repeated salvos needed to correct fall of shot. Surviving figures may come from sales claims, technical manuals, or later recollection after original records were destroyed, so nominal performance requires source criticism.

evidence.note: The opening discusses 16.5-inch gun appeal, initial versus sustained firing rates, and the reliability of technical performance claims.

segments.summary: The recurring 16.5-inch proposal opens a practical lesson about shell weight, sustained rate of fire, and caution with advertised gun statistics.

segments.title: Why unbuilt capital ships are revealing
segments.body: The video groups capital-ship designs by the historical moment that stopped them instead of treating every cancelled ship as one category. The end of the First World War, the Washington treaty settlement, treaty-era planning, and renewed prewar construction each provide a different sampling point. Paper projects preserve the direction in which designers and institutions intended to move before budgets, treaties, infrastructure, and war forced compromises. Comparing those projects exposes strategic ambition and the limits that kept it from becoming a completed ship.

evidence.note: The introduction explains why cancelled capital-ship projects are a useful historical sample.

segments.summary: Unbuilt designs preserve a navy's ambitions before war, treaties, industry, and budgets forced compromises.

segments.title: Germany's L20 and the appeal of 16.5-inch guns
segments.body: The L20 was Germany's much more direct answer to the Queen Elizabeth class in this interpretation, rather than the slower Bayern class. Its proposed 26-knot speed and eight 16.5-inch guns sought to meet British advantages in mobility, protection, and firepower with a single fast battleship. German expectations that Britain would make a similar jump turned gun size into an anticipatory arms-race decision. The transcript also advances a speculative British counter-design: knowledge of German development may have encouraged a proposed sixth Queen Elizabeth-class ship armed with six 18-inch guns. The comparison combines a plausible German technical response with the intelligence-driven pressure to outguess the next capital ship.

evidence.note: The transcript describes L20's proposed armament and speed as a response to Queen Elizabeth.

segments.summary: The L20 project illustrates a German response to the Queen Elizabeth class built around 26-knot speed and 16.5-inch guns.

segments.title: Mackensen, Ersatz Yorck, and Germany's battlecruiser problem
segments.body: Mackensen and Ersatz Yorck sit on a spectrum where increasing armament and protection bring the battlecruiser progressively closer to the battleship. Their roughly 27-28-knot speeds were too close to the proposed 26-knot L20 battle line to secure the decisive mobility advantage a battlecruiser needed. They also could not reliably outrun British battlecruisers or replace heavily armed battleships in a fleet action. Because Germany devoted scarce yards, engines, material, and design effort to both types, the projects illustrate a force-structure problem: copying British categories displaced investment from the faster battle line Germany's circumstances arguably required. Germany's ocean-liner industry offered relevant high-speed engineering experience that could have reinforced a fast-battleship programme. Zeppelin reconnaissance also weakened the case for consuming capital-ship yards and resources merely to obtain scouting information.

evidence.note: Comparison of Mackensen and Ersatz Yorck with German battleship needs, ocean-liner engineering, Zeppelin reconnaissance, and strategic speed.

segments.summary: Mackensen and Ersatz Yorck expose a mismatch between German battlecruiser investment and the battle-line role Germany needed to strengthen.

segments.title: Why submarine success cannot be read from sinkings alone
segments.body: A substantial aside challenges the assumption that Germany should simply have transferred capital-ship resources to submarines. First World War U-boats came closer to a strategic decision partly because anti-submarine warfare was still developing, whereas the Second World War Allies built intelligence, escort, and hunting systems that generally kept pace. The rise in 1942 sinkings shows why operational context matters: escorts and hunting groups were diverted to protect Operation Torch convoys, temporarily weakening other routes without making each U-boat intrinsically more lethal. Histories centred on attacked convoys can also obscure the many sailings that passed without contact.

evidence.note: The transcript compares U-boat effectiveness across the world wars and links part of the 1942 increase to escorts diverted for Operation Torch.

segments.summary: A comparison of the two world wars shows how anti-submarine systems and the temporary diversion of escorts shaped apparent U-boat success.

segments.title: Austro-Hungarian design for the Adriatic
segments.body: Austria-Hungary's geography made control of the Adriatic its first naval problem, not distant oceanic operations. A fleet unable to defeat or contain Italy could not reach the wider Mediterranean, so overseas ambitions had to follow regional sea control rather than precede it. The proposed Ersatz Monarch class was a more capable continuation of a navy designed around that concrete mission. The contrast with German battlecruisers is institutional as well as technical: the Austro-Hungarian design begins with the fleet's operating problem instead of copying a British blue-water category.

evidence.note: The transcript links Austrian naval construction to the need to control and escape the Adriatic.

segments.summary: The Ersatz Monarch concept is used to show a fleet designed around controlling the Adriatic before seeking wider influence.

segments.title: Russian capital ships for a Black Sea risk fleet
segments.body: The repeated Russian layout of four triple turrets on the centreline is presented as a practical answer to limited money, technology, and strategic reach. The programme drew on Italian and British technology while keeping the same basic arrangement across several classes. These ships were unlikely to meet Japan's battle fleet or Germany's Baltic strength on equal terms, but they could still impose enough risk to complicate an attack. Their more attainable task was to dominate the Black Sea, overmatch the Ottoman fleet, and protect Russian access to maritime routes. Standardized evolution therefore mattered more than novelty because it kept construction within a technological pace Russia could afford and maintain.

evidence.note: Imported technology, Russian constraints, Black Sea aims, and a risk-fleet approach.

segments.summary: Russian designs are read as an affordable regional fleet: deter stronger opponents, dominate the Black Sea, and preserve access to it.

segments.title: What completed Borodinos might have changed
segments.body: One or two completed Borodino battlecruisers could have given the Soviet Union faster, better-protected capital ships than the surviving Ganguts. With twelve 14-inch guns and roughly 26-27 knots, they would have offered a mobile instrument rather than a slow inherited battle line. Their location during the revolution and civil war could also have affected the balance between Red and White naval forces. In the longer term, operational experience with them might have changed Soviet doctrine and encouraged Japanese pressure to include the Soviet Union in interwar naval-treaty calculations.

evidence.note: Borodino speed, protection, and possible Soviet-era consequences.

segments.summary: The Borodino battlecruisers offer a counterfactual route to a more mobile early Soviet capital-ship doctrine.

segments.title: Francesco Caracciolo and the cost of 28 knots
segments.body: The Italian project moved from four triple turrets to five twins and finally four twin 15-inch turrets so that speed, armour, and torpedo defence could coexist. That reduction in gun count was a deliberate exchange, not evidence that the concept had failed. The resulting 28-knot ship would have combined decisive mobility with the protection needed to stay in a fleet action, making Francesco Caracciolo an early fast-battleship benchmark. In this counterfactual, even limited completion could have accelerated French and British responses and given later Italian designs a much stronger starting point.

evidence.note: The transcript traces the Caracciolo armament reductions made to retain speed and protection.

segments.summary: The Caracciolo design shows Italy sacrificing gun numbers in order to preserve protection and a 28-knot fast-battleship concept.

segments.title: Why 28 knots mattered in the Mediterranean
segments.body: The video distinguishes the Mediterranean requirement from the open-ocean battlecruiser ideal. Italy could not use speed simply to avoid combat because access to the wider sea depended on fighting within a confined theatre. A 28-knot battleship could instead choose when to engage and still carry enough armour and firepower to finish the fight. The seven-knot advantage over a 21-knot battle line becomes decisive mobility, and Caracciolo might even have supplied the name and standard for a new fast-battleship generation. The counterfactual then asks whether Britain would still build N3s to seal Gibraltar, although fixed coastal guns might perform that mission without placing a capital ship at the chokepoint. The comparison shows how answering a foreign fast battleship could redirect ship design, basing, and diplomacy toward Spain as well as change fleet speed.

evidence.note: The Mediterranean case for speed combined with decisive protection and firepower.

segments.summary: In an enclosed sea, speed has to help decide and finish a fight rather than merely avoid it.

segments.title: G3 and N3 at opposite ends of the capital-ship spectrum
segments.body: The G3 and N3 were related but fundamentally different answers to post-Jutland requirements. G3's turret and superstructure arrangement might still have changed during construction because the framing allowed variants closer to the F3 or later Nelson layout. The G3 accepted 16.5-inch guns and concentrated machinery weight to preserve very high speed, while the 18-inch-gunned N3 was designed as an exceptionally resilient brawler. Together they define opposite ends of the capital-ship spectrum and show how the Royal Navy translated Jutland's protection lessons into two different operational tools.

evidence.note: The transcript compares G3 flexibility and speed with N3 firepower, protection, and endurance.

segments.summary: The G3 prioritises high strategic mobility, while the N3 is portrayed as the most heavily armed and protected battleship its generation could produce.

segments.title: When more armour can make a shell more destructive
segments.body: At extreme gun calibres, adding armour can cease to be an automatic answer because thick structure may simply give an incoming shell material in which to detonate. Once weapons exceed roughly 18 inches, this argument places more weight on internal subdivision, watertightness, and many small compartments that confine damage. The N3 still represents the armoured-battleship extreme of its generation, built to absorb repeated punishment while returning 18-inch fire. The watch point separates protection philosophy from a simple thickness contest and shows why designers have to balance resistance, damage localisation, and weapon effects.

evidence.note: The transcript weighs armour against honeycombed internal subdivision when very large shells can turn protective structure into detonation material.

segments.summary: Against shells larger than 18 inches, survival may depend less on ever-thicker armour and more on subdivision that confines flooding and blast damage.

segments.title: Hood, G3, and the meaning of battlecruiser
segments.body: The discussion places Hood, Renown, and the G3s at different points on a design spectrum rather than treating armour thickness or gun calibre as a complete classification. Renown and Repulse remain closer to the traditional two-word battle cruiser built around strategic mobility, while Hood was an earlier design modified after Jutland toward heavier protection. In the video's terminology, G3 was conceived from the outset to combine exceptional speed with the ability to defeat other major cruisers, making it the more mature one-word battlecruiser concept. A German account of HMS Rodney reaching roughly 26 knots while pursuing them despite her 23-knot design figure provides practical evidence for conservative British speed estimates. Because G3 and N3 used related hull thinking, both cancelled classes might likewise have exceeded their paper speeds, sharpening the distinction between them and foreign projects.

evidence.note: The transcript positions Hood, Renown, G3, and N3 along a battleship-to-battlecruiser spectrum and considers likely speed margins.

segments.summary: Hood's post-Jutland improvements do not, in this argument, make it equivalent to the purpose-designed G3 battlecruisers.

segments.title: The uncertain names of the G3 and N3 classes
segments.body: Proposed names for the G3 and N3 classes provide an example of academic whispers. A cautious recollection in a generally reliable source can be copied repeatedly until later writers present it as settled fact. Royal Navy naming practice and the political implausibility of invoking Ireland's patron saint as Ireland left the union both weigh against the common saint-class claim. Admirals, battles, virtues, or a revived Dreadnought remain possibilities, but the main learning point is methodological: plausible repetition is not the same as documentary confirmation.

evidence.note: The transcript critiques repeated naming claims and compares them with Royal Navy naming practice and contemporary politics.

segments.summary: Claims about saint names for the cancelled British classes illustrate how tentative recollections can harden into accepted naval history.

segments.title: South Dakota and Lexington as a fleet system
segments.body: An inserted correction warns that repeated spoken references to the North Dakota class in this section mean the planned 1920 South Dakota class. Those battleships supply the battle line's destructive weight, while the Lexingtons locate the enemy and give that concentrated force operational reach. The analogy makes the battleships a hammerhead and the battlecruisers the shaft that directs it. This pairing was especially suited to Pacific distances, where the United States expected room to manoeuvre and could organise around a concentrated fleet. The comparison with G3 also shows why similar-looking fast ships can serve different systems: British battlecruisers had worldwide trade and imperial tasks, whereas Lexington primarily enabled the American battle line.

evidence.note: The South Dakotas as battle-line power and Lexingtons as the force that finds the enemy.

segments.summary: The cancelled American South Dakotas and Lexingtons are read as complementary heavy battle-line and scouting forces for Pacific operations.

segments.title: How one fast battleship could trigger several foreign responses
segments.body: The possible completion of Francesco Caracciolo shows why naval arms races rarely proceed as a simple two-country duel. Britain would have to consider Italian power in the Mediterranean, France would respond to Italy, and Britain would then have to account for the French response as well as its own imperial route through the enclosed sea. Once Britain adjusted, other powers would reinterpret their own requirements and programmes. The chain is a compact lesson in international relations: procurement decisions can propagate through alliances, rivalries, geography, and uncertainty even when the original ship is not aimed directly at every respondent.

evidence.note: The transcript traces how an Italian fast battleship could prompt French and British responses and then wider international reactions.

segments.summary: A completed Francesco Caracciolo could have pushed France and Britain into linked responses, showing why naval competition spreads through more than one pair of rivals.

segments.title: Japan's Eight-Eight fleet meets yard capacity
segments.body: The Japanese Eight-Eight programme charts several future generations, from Tosa and Amagi through the Kii and Number 13 classes. The sequence also reveals a doctrinal transition: Amagi remains a battlecruiser, while the later 30-knot designs converge on fast battleships with 16.1-inch and then 18-inch guns. On the video's estimate, limited slips and shallow supporting yard capacity would have pushed the final ships toward the late 1920s even if everything went well. The programme records a coherent aspiration while showing why industrial depth and earthquake-vulnerable infrastructure mattered as much as the drawings themselves.

evidence.note: The transcript covers the Japanese construction sequence, intended roles, and limits of yard capacity.

segments.summary: Japan's sequence from Amagi through Number 13 reveals both a coherent fast-battleship direction and the industrial bottleneck that constrained it.

segments.title: Why Britain's post-G3 plans remain uncertain
segments.body: Britain's next capital ship after the G3 and N3 classes had not yet become a settled design. An 18-inch fast battleship is plausible, and a 16.5-inch alternative also fits the direction under discussion. The Royal Navy was still waiting for trials, policy decisions, and experience from the ships already planned, so contemporary officials could not know the final answer themselves. Later reconstructions can propose likely paths, but certainty exceeds the surviving evidence.

evidence.note: The transcript says post-G3 and post-N3 British plans were unsettled because later choices depended on policy, testing, and results that were not yet available.

segments.summary: British plans after the G3 and N3 classes were still fluid, so later claims of a definite successor design should be treated cautiously.

segments.title: How institutions shaped British, American, and Japanese ship plans
segments.body: Different procurement institutions explain why surviving paper fleets have different levels of detail. Japan had to plan far ahead because limited yards and infrastructure made each construction sequence consequential, while the United States needed firmer proposals to obtain congressional authorisation and manage political intervention. The Royal Navy could keep later designs fluid, present recommendations through ministers and cabinet channels, and sometimes use secrecy to cover decisions still awaiting trials. The argument supports civilian control over whether a fleet requirement should be funded, but warns that detailed political substitution of guns and specifications can produce a design by committee instead of returning the requirement to naval professionals for revision.

evidence.note: The transcript contrasts congressional, cabinet, and infrastructure-driven planning and discusses the boundary between civilian oversight and detailed ship specification.

segments.summary: Different approval systems explain why Japan planned generations ahead, Congress demanded firmer American proposals, and Britain could keep designs fluid and secret.

segments.title: Normandie, Lyon, and French design momentum
segments.body: In this assessment, the sixteen-gun Lyon had more potential than Normandie, but both remained tied to 13.4-inch weapons and 21-knot speed as foreign standards advanced. France might have sought British 15-inch gun technology instead of compounding the risks of a new quadruple turret with an increasingly modest calibre. Political interference and individual yards' departures from central designs further weakened the connection between national capability and the ships delivered. The Washington settlement consequently becomes a beneficial pause that broke procurement momentum and allowed France to reset before the more coherent Dunkerque generation.

evidence.note: The transcript critiques the French projects' armament, speed, and procurement context.

segments.summary: The Normandie and Lyon projects illustrate the danger of continuing an established design path after rivals have changed the standard.

segments.title: Plan Z and the limits of German rearmament
segments.body: The O-class battlecruisers could reach about 35 knots, but aircraft reconnaissance and land-based air power narrowed the sea room in which speed alone could evade combat. A defender moving to intercept a known destination could cover a shorter distance, so fast battleships and air attack could force the engagement the raider was built to avoid. H39 is treated as a more credible battleship, yet its eight 16-inch guns compared poorly with Britain's nine-gun Lion at similar speed and exposed Germany's conservative industrial ceiling. The argument traces part of that ceiling to British priorities at Versailles: more than reparations, Britain wanted to cripple the maritime industry and infrastructure that could sustain another German fleet. Plan Z also multiplied 15-inch, 16-inch, 16.5-inch, and prospective 18-inch ammunition systems, making heavy-gun logistics another way the programme could defeat itself.

evidence.note: The transcript evaluates Plan Z, O-class mobility, H39, the Versailles attack on German maritime capacity, and the programme's heavy-gun logistics.

segments.summary: Plan Z's O-class and H-class proposals are tested against British opposition, aircraft reconnaissance, industrial limits, and the difficulty of sustaining several gun calibres.

segments.title: Yamato and the ultimate-weapon trap
segments.body: In this reading, Japan answered limited shipbuilding capacity by pursuing decisive qualitative superiority through Yamato and the still larger A-150 ideas. Such an ultimate weapon could create short-term uncertainty or even push an exposed American battle fleet back from Pearl Harbor if its capabilities became known before war. The advantage would be temporary because Britain and the United States could revive 18-inch and 16.5-inch studies, then build improved counters in greater numbers from deeper industrial bases. Japan's expensive leap would therefore provoke the kind of competition its infrastructure was least able to sustain, turning a bid for security into a long-term strategic trap.

evidence.note: Why an ultimate weapon produces countermeasures and worsens Japan's infrastructure problem.

segments.summary: A super-battleship may offer a short-lived advantage, but it can also provoke better-resourced rivals to build an effective counter.

segments.title: Why nuclear weapons deter without guaranteeing victory
segments.body: The claim that no weapon remains ultimate is briefly tested against nuclear arms. Another nuclear arsenal or a strike on the launch system can counter them, while their destructive effects may also make use self-defeating. Nuclear weapons may prevent an opponent from winning, but they do not necessarily provide a usable path to one's own victory because both sides can lose together. The aside connects the super-battleship argument to deterrence theory: unmatched destructive power can alter choices without delivering positive strategic control.

evidence.note: The transcript explains that nuclear weapons can stop the other side winning while leaving both sides able to lose together.

segments.summary: Nuclear arms can deny an opponent victory, yet their self-destructive consequences make them an imperfect example of an ultimate weapon.

segments.title: Montana, Iowa, and an enduring American doctrine
segments.body: The Montana studies range along the battleship end of the capital-ship spectrum, while some Iowa paper variants approach the fast-battleship or even one-word battlecruiser boundary. Their roles preserve a consistent American logic rather than creating rival categories for their own sake. Montana supplies the heavily protected battle line intended to absorb punishment, return repeatedly, and deny an opponent a decisive result. Iowa provides the mobile component, updating the earlier South Dakota-Lexington relationship within a simple force structure designed to keep advancing across oceanic distances. The wider procurement lesson is that a simple doctrine consistently matched to national needs can be smarter than novelty because fewer moving parts leave fewer ways for a force structure to fail.

evidence.note: The transcript places Montana and Iowa within a consistent American capital-ship doctrine.

segments.summary: Montana and Iowa update the same American division between a resilient battle line and mobile supporting forces.

segments.title: British global commitments and the Lion class
segments.body: The video contrasts the American concentration of force with Britain's need to move between distant theatres and retain freedom of action across a worldwide empire. That geography made strategic speed more important to the Royal Navy, while still demanding the protection of a battleship rather than an interwar raider. In this assessment, the nine-gun, roughly 30-knot Lion is a strong baseline that could have followed the King George V class and challenged German designs on equal terms. Lion, a King George V variant using established 15-inch guns, or F3-derived 28-knot ships are all preferred to the historical ten-gun arrangement because each alternative would have changed foreign calculations. Lion's aircraft facilities also introduce a transitional question: spotting remained valuable, but Britain was already considering whether carrier-based aircraft could remove fuel and aviation spaces from the capital ship itself.

evidence.note: The transcript connects British global strategy, American planning, and the Lion fast-battleship design.

segments.summary: Britain needed speed for a worldwide empire, but the proposed Lions show why fast battleships - not battlecruisers - became the preferred answer.

segments.title: What Anglo-American war plans did - and did not - mean
segments.body: British and American interwar contingency plans do not by themselves prove that either government expected war. Each navy used the other first-rate power as the hardest planning and exercise problem, because preparing against a lesser opponent would test less of the staff and fleet. An informal diplomatic anecdote in which Halifax's shared importance was discussed almost humorously illustrates how closely the two states communicated while their staffs examined conflict. A real war would have been mutually ruinous: Britain could threaten both American coasts, while U.S. concentration would expose long logistics lines and dispersion would dilute the fleet's central strength. Senior review comments also focused more on planning method in the Anglo-American case, whereas plans involving Japan, Italy, or France drew greater attention to operational content, so the documents must be interpreted in their institutional context.

evidence.note: The transcript explains contingency planning as a demanding staff exercise, describes continuing diplomacy, and contrasts how senior officers reviewed different war plans.

segments.summary: Planning against the strongest available opponent tested staffs and fleets, but sustained diplomatic contact makes those plans poor evidence of an expected Anglo-American war.

segments.title: Aircraft spotting and the declining battlecruiser role
segments.body: Spotting aircraft allow a battleship to correct repeated salvos and deliver far more explosive weight than a single aircraft load. The unresolved question was whether fuel, aircraft, and handling facilities had to remain on the capital ship once a carrier air group could provide the same eyes. Treaty limits and the need to keep carriers survivable initially constrained the number of aircraft available for fleet support. As carrier capacity matured, fast battleships could cover the fighting role while carrier aircraft supplied the very-high-speed scouting and reach once associated with battlecruisers. North Sea weather imposed a practical limit on deck parking: one 1920s incident made the sea the Fleet Air Arm's largest source of aircraft losses.

evidence.note: Comparison of capital-ship spotting aircraft with carrier air groups, treaty-limited carrier survivability, North Sea deck parking, and the declining battlecruiser role.

segments.summary: Aircraft could extend a battleship's gunnery reach, while carrier aviation increasingly supplied the high-speed scouting role once assigned to battlecruisers.

segments.title: Soviet battleship and battlecruiser ambitions
segments.body: A late-1930s battleship baseline of roughly 28 knots with 16-inch guns helps map the Soviet projects from battleship through battlecruiser to heavy cruiser. Stalingrad's 12-inch battery and very high speed place it closer to the Alaska or an unconstrained heavy cruiser than to a classic capital-ship brawler. The discussion of hypothetical 20-inch weapons explains why calibre alone is misleading: a slow sustained firing cycle gives an opponent more ranging salvos and may surrender the chance to hit first. Although Project 23, Stalingrad, and related ships were unlikely to be completed quickly, together they reveal Stalin's aim for a balanced fleet and the international status and security of a seat at the great-power table.

evidence.note: Soviet capital-ship roles, calibre tradeoffs, and the political aim of a balanced fleet.

segments.summary: Soviet projects for battleships, battlecruisers, and heavy cruisers are interpreted as a bid for a balanced fleet and international status.

segments.title: Unbuilt warships as a record of national ambition
segments.body: A completed ship is the result of compromise with industrial capacity, infrastructure, politics, available technology, and the weapons a yard can actually manufacture. Scharnhorst and Gneisenau provide the closing example: Germany wanted 15-inch guns but initially had to accept 11-inch weapons. Unbuilt projects preserve the less compromised aspiration and therefore reveal what navies feared, desired, and believed their future fleets should accomplish. Comparing dream with delivery turns cancelled designs into evidence about national ambition as well as the practical systems that prevented ambition from becoming steel.

evidence.note: The closing summary explains how unbuilt ships reveal aspirations constrained by reality.

segments.summary: The conclusion returns to the central lesson: cancelled designs show the gap between what navies wanted and what their resources allowed.
